opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'm a theorist, so I should say up front that I don't build these things myself. I'm the guy who sits on the sidelines and tells the experimentalists what they should be trying to do, and then they tell me it's much harder than I think. But I can tell you how I understand the challenge.

The fundamental problem is this: a quantum computer needs to keep qubits in superposition and entanglement, and it needs to manipulate them with exquisite precision. At the same time, it has to keep them almost perfectly isolated from the outside world. Any stray interaction with the environment is effectively a measurement. The environment "learns" something about the state of your qubits, and that destroys the delicate interference effects you're relying on. That's decoherence. So you have this tension. You want the qubits to talk to each other and to your control apparatus, but you don't want them talking to anything else in the universe. That turns out to be enormously hard.

For a long time, people thought this might be a fundamental obstacle. In the mid-1990s, right after Peter Shor discovered his factoring algorithm, a lot of skeptics said, look, you can never get the noise low enough, and errors will just accumulate. What changed the picture was the discovery of quantum error correction and the threshold theorem. Shor, Steane, Aharonov and Ben-Or, Kitaev, Knill, Laflamme, and Zurek all contributed. The upshot is that if you can get the physical error rate per operation below some threshold, then you can encode logical qubits across many physical qubits. You can then detect and correct errors faster than they accumulate, and compute for as long as you want. So in principle, the problem goes from impossible to a question of engineering.

But of course "just engineering" can hide a lot. To do fault-tolerant computation, you might need hundreds or thousands of physical qubits for every logical qubit, depending on the error rates and the code. And to run something like Shor's algorithm on cryptographically relevant key sizes, you'd want thousands of logical qubits. So now you're talking about potentially millions of physical qubits, all controlled with high fidelity, with fast classical processing to decode the error syndromes in real time.

There are multiple hardware approaches competing right now. There are superconducting qubits, which Google and IBM have pursued. There are trapped ions, with companies like Quantinuum and IonQ. There are neutral atoms held in optical tweezers, photonics, and the topological approach that Microsoft has been betting on. Each has its own tradeoffs. Ions have beautiful fidelities and all-to-all connectivity, but they're slow, and scaling up is hard. Superconducting qubits are fast, but they need dilution refrigerators, and the wiring becomes a nightmare. Neutral atoms have made really striking progress lately in scaling up qubit counts.

What's been exciting to me over the last few years is that we've finally started to see experiments demonstrating error correction actually working as advertised. As you make the code bigger, the logical error rate goes down rather than up. That was always the key prediction of the theory, and for decades it was just a prediction. Now we're seeing it in the lab. So I've gone from saying "this is possible in principle" to saying the remaining obstacles look like hard engineering problems, not like some new physics that will block us. I've always said that if it turned out quantum computing were impossible for some deep reason, that would be even more exciting than building one, because it would mean quantum mechanics is wrong or incomplete. But so far nature hasn't given us that out.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that it's fundamentally different from the engineering task of building a classical computer, and the reason comes down to one word: decoherence. A quantum computer only works if your qubits are isolated from their environment to an almost absurd degree. The moment a qubit leaks information about its state to the outside world, you've effectively measured it, and the quantum superposition that was doing all the work collapses. So you're trying to build a machine that is simultaneously exquisitely controllable by you and completely invisible to everything else in the universe. Those two requirements pull in opposite directions, and that tension is basically the whole engineering problem.

Now, the great theoretical result from the mid-nineties, which is really the reason anyone is spending billions of dollars on this, is quantum error correction and the threshold theorem. What that says is that you don't need perfect qubits. If you can get your physical error rates below some threshold, maybe one in a thousand per operation or so depending on the scheme, then in principle you can encode one logical qubit redundantly across many physical qubits and correct errors faster than they accumulate. Without that result, I think the whole enterprise would have been hopeless, because nobody is ever going to build a perfectly isolated qubit.

But "in principle" is doing a lot of work in that sentence. The overheads are enormous. You might need a thousand physical qubits for every logical qubit you actually want to compute with. So when people ask me how it's going, I tell them to watch two numbers: how many qubits you have, and how good they are. For a long time those traded off against each other. You could have a few very good qubits or many mediocre ones. What's been exciting in the last few years is that we've started to see demonstrations where adding more physical qubits to an error-correcting code actually makes the logical qubit better rather than worse. That's the sign you're on the right side of the threshold, and I honestly didn't know whether I'd see that in my career.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that we still don't know which hardware platform wins. Superconducting qubits, trapped ions, neutral atoms, photonics, maybe topological qubits if those ever pan out. They have completely different strengths. It's a bit like being in the 1940s and not knowing whether computers would be built from vacuum tubes or relays or something no one had invented yet. So I try to be humble about timelines. I think the physics is sound, I think the path is clear in outline, and I think the remaining obstacles are the kind that engineers solve rather than the kind that require a miracle. But "engineers can solve it" and "it will be solved soon" are very different claims, and I only feel confident about the first one.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as the task of creating a system of quantum bits that we can control extremely precisely while keeping them sufficiently isolated from their environment. Those requirements pull in opposite directions: we need to interact with the qubits to perform computations and read out answers, but unwanted interactions can destroy the quantum information. That’s the problem of decoherence.

The remarkable thing is that quantum error correction gives us a way forward. You can encode a logical qubit across many physical qubits, detect errors without learning the information you’re trying to protect, and correct them. If the underlying operations are accurate enough, then, in principle, you can keep a computation going for as long as you need.

So the engineering challenge is to get below those error thresholds and then scale up, with all the control systems and error correction that requires. It’s an enormous challenge, but we have a theoretical framework that explains why it should be possible. The question is whether we can make that framework work efficiently in real hardware.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as the task of building a system that you can control extremely precisely, while keeping it almost completely isolated from its environment. And those demands pull in opposite directions: you need to interact with the qubits to manipulate them and read out an answer, but unwanted interactions can destroy the quantum information you’re trying to preserve.

The central challenge is error correction. You shouldn’t imagine that we need to build a machine where nothing ever goes wrong. Instead, we need physical qubits whose errors are sufficiently small and sufficiently well behaved that we can encode information across many of them, detect errors, and correct them faster than they accumulate—without measuring and destroying the computation itself.

So this is an enormous engineering problem, but it has a theoretical foundation: quantum fault tolerance tells us that, under the right conditions, reliable computation is possible with unreliable components. The engineering task is to actually reach those conditions and then scale up.
